name_note — removed on audit: Prose is accurate but the third sub-claim is effectively uncited — its citation carries the wrong quote. Sub-claim by sub-claim, verified live: (1) "NC State leads with 'Canadian Wild Ginger'" — COVERED AND ACCURATE, citation 1 quote is verbatim from the page title. (2) "Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder leads with 'wild ginger'" — COVERED AND ACCURATE; MOBOT kempercode=b460 is the Asarum canadense page and its field reads verbatim "Common Name: wild ginger". (3) "RHS's own page title/lead uses 'Canada wild ginger'" — UNCITED BUT TRUE. Its citation (citation 3) attaches the quote "Full shade, Partial shade", which is RHS's Position field and says nothing whatsoever about a common name; the quote does not support the claim it is filed under. The fact is real: RHS's H1 reads "Asarum canadense | Canada wild ginger". Notably "Canada wild ginger" appears ONLY in that H1/lead — RHS's own Common Names list on the same page runs "Black snakeweed, Canadian snakeroot, colic root, false crowfoot, ginger root, heart-leaf, pigs, snake root, southern snakeroot, southern wild ginger, Vermont snakeroot" and does not contain it — so the field's careful wording "page title/lead" is precise and should be kept. No sub-claim is WRONG; nothing needs dropping. Repair is citation-only: keep the name_note prose exactly as written and replace citation 3's quote with the page H1, "Asarum canadense | Canada wild ginger".

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The field PROSE is correct and complete — the defect is that its only supporting NC State citation truncates the load-bearing safety list, so the field asserts more than its evidence covers. Citation 6's quote ends "...Poison Part: Leaves". The live page reads "Poison Part: Leaves, Roots, Stems". The field text itself correctly says "Poison Part: Leaves, Roots, Stems", but no citation in the record supports "Roots, Stems" — a truncated safety quote on the rhizome, which is the part people actually dig up and taste as a ginger substitute, is the worst possible place to trim. Repair is citation-only: replace citation 6's quote tail with the page's real text, "Poison Part: Leaves, Roots, Stems". Everything else in the field verifies verbatim and is complete: Poison Severity "Medium" (correctly scoped in the prose as coming from the human-scoped "Poisonous to Humans" block), the full symptom text "Aristolochic acid is nephrotoxic and a carcinogen. Do not consume any part of this plant." with no dose sentence dropped, Poison Toxic Principle "Aristolochic acid", Causes Contact Dermatitis "No", and the verified absence of any Problem-for-Cats / Problem-for-Dogs tag on the NC State page. The RHS "Potentially harmful" text is reproduced verbatim and correctly, including the handling warning "Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" — which is retained rather than softened even though NC State says Causes Contact Dermatitis: No, and the field puts the two adjacent so the tension is visible. The pets-scope disagreement is disclosed and reasoned. The source's own hazard words (nephrotoxic, carcinogen, TOXIC if eaten) are preserved rather than paraphrased.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The facts are true but the safety field is trimmed and softened in three ways, and one of its citations overreaches. (1) SOFTENED HAZARD, own-words rule: the field paraphrases NC State's Edibility entry as "young shoots and rootstock are edible after boiling", dropping the source's actual preparation requirement. NC State's real sentence is "Young shoots can be boiled for 10 minutes.  Rootstock can be eaten after boiled for 20 minutes." The specific durations are the load-bearing part of an edibility-of-a-poisonous-plant note and must not be paraphrased away. (2) INCOMPLETE TAG LIST: NC State's Whole Plant Traits > Plant Type carries four tags — "Herbaceous Perennial / Native Plant / Poisonous / Wildflower" — and the field names only "Poisonous". Citation #8 compounds this: its quote "Poisonous\nWildflower" is a genuine contiguous slice but is only 2 of the 4 tags, presented as though it were the tag list. (3) CITATION #8 CLAIM/QUOTE MISMATCH: the claim asserts NC State "lists a 'Poisonous' Whole Plant Trait alongside an Edibility note describing the plant as also edible after preparation", but the quote contains no Edibility text whatsoever — the quote does not say what the claim asserts. (4) UNDISCLOSED SOURCE DISAGREEMENT ON PART SCOPE: NC State confines the hazard to fruit — "Poison Part: Fruits", and its Fruit Description reads "Blue-black inedible (to humans) berries are very showy and appear in September to October, are blue-black and 1/4 to 1/2 inch wide." — whereas RHS's warning is unrestricted ("Harmful if eaten", plus a handling warning implying whole-plant contact). The field discloses the human-vs-pet scope disagreement but not this part-scope disagreement. What IS correct and should be kept: the verbatim NC State Poisonous to Humans block (#7 verified exactly, including the complete symptom list "Vomiting, diarrhea." — there is no dose sentence at NC State to omit); the explicit statement that the Low severity rating is human-scoped and separate from any cat/dog field (accurate — NC State has no pet field); and the full verbatim RHS string, which correctly carries the "Wear gloves and and other protective equipment when handling" handling warning. SUGGESTED REPAIR: replace the Edibility paraphrase with NC State's verbatim sentence, list all four Plant Type tags (Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant, Poisonous, Wildflower), re-quote citation #8 against the real Edibility text rather than the 2-tag slice, and add one clause noting that NC State scopes the poison to Fruits while RHS's warning is unrestricted.

outdoor_sun_exposure — FLAGGED on audit (left as-is, needs manual review before landing): DROP "full_sun"; KEEP "part_shade" and "full_shade". part_shade and full_shade are unanimous and cleanly cited: RHS Position lists "Full shade / Full sun / Partial shade"; MOBOT's structured field is "Sun: Part shade to full shade"; NC State's Light field is "Deep shade (Less than 2 hours to no direct sunlight)" and "Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)". full_sun rests on exactly one source and is contradicted by the structured sun field of both others. NC State's Light field lists only Deep shade and Partial Shade — full sun is absent, and NC State's own description prose bounds it the same way: "Plant it in medium to wet average soil in partial to full shade, though it does best with some sun." MOBOT's structured Sun field is "Part shade to full shade" and its Culture sentence — the very sentence this record quotes for soil_base — says "in part shade to full shade". So the record quotes a MOBOT sentence that excludes full sun while simultaneously asserting full sun from RHS. The lone support is RHS, whose guidance is UK-climate-calibrated (the same page states its ratings "refer to the UK growing conditions unless otherwise stated"), for a plant that both North American sources treat as a woodland-shade understory perennial. Citation #9 is not itself fabricated — RHS's Position field and Cultivation prose genuinely do list full sun unconditionally, and the quote is verbatim — but a 2-of-3 structured-field contradiction puts the value in genuine doubt for a US-facing care app, where advising full sun for a shade woodland perennial is a real care risk. Additionally, this disagreement is disclosed nowhere in the record: neither name_note nor unknowns mentions that NC State and MOBOT exclude full sun. If full_sun is retained over this objection, that disagreement must at minimum be surfaced in a note.

outdoor_sun_exposure narrowed to part_shade and full_shade: only RHS lists full sun; NC State's Light field carries Deep shade and Partial Shade only, and MOBOT's structured field is 'Sun: Part shade to full shade' -- both North American sources treat it as a woodland-shade perennial.

records.cool_rest_note: Spring ephemeral: foliage dies to the ground and the plant goes fully dormant by mid-summer after flowering (NC State: "The foliage dies to the ground in mid-summer, and the plant becomes dormant."; Missouri Botanical Garden: "Foliage dies to the ground by mid-summer as the plant goes dormant."). No admissible source gives care guidance for the dormant period itself (e.g. whether/how much to water while dormant).
records.name_note: NC State Extension's dedicated page lists its common names alphabetically starting with 'Blue and Pink Ladies' rather than by a stated primary name (its twelve-name list includes 'Virginia Bluebells'). Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated page states a single primary name, 'Virginia bluebells', and RHS leads with the near-identical spelling variant 'Virginian bluebells' -- 'Virginia bluebells' is used here on that basis.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: NC State's page for Mertensia virginica carries no Poison/toxicity section, and RHS's dedicated page carries no 'Potentially harmful' field for this species. No admissible source addresses cat/dog toxicity for this species at all.

soil_ph left null: sources disagree on how tightly bounded the pH range is. Penn State Extension's rain-garden page states 'Neutral (pH 6.8 to 7.2)' for this species specifically, but RHS's pH field for the same species lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (i.e., alkaline soils are also acceptable), and NC State's Soil pH tags likewise span Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0), and Alkaline (>8.0) bands. Given RHS and NC State both indicate a wider tolerance than Penn State's narrow range, no reliable ceiling/floor is set.

outdoor_sun_exposure: Penn State Extension's rain-garden page gives a structured 'Sun: Sun/partial shade' field, which could suggest full-sun tolerance, but this conflicts with NC State (Deep shade to Partial Shade only), Missouri Botanical Garden ('Part shade to full shade'), and RHS ('Partial shade' only) — none of which list full sun. Because the majority of dedicated sources describe this as a shade/part-shade woodland species with no unconditional full-sun statement corroborated elsewhere, full_sun and part_sun were not added to outdoor_sun_exposure.

No admissible source gives a foot-candle light range, a temperature range (day/night), a humidity target, a fertilizing schedule, or a watering interval/dry-down depth for this species — these fields are left null.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are left null because this is an in-ground garden perennial and no admissible source frames watering in terms of a dry-down target or day interval.

Penn State Extension's rain-garden page separately notes the species is 'Moist, inundation tolerant' under a 'Hydrologic zone' field (i.e., tolerates occasional flooding in a rain-garden context), consistent with the 'moderate' soil_drainage reading (occasionally wet tolerated alongside a well-drained preference) rather than indicating a consistently wet/boggy requirement.

name_note — removed on audit: The value contains a false statement. The note justifies the choice by saying "it is the name led by two of the three single-species dedicated pages (Missouri Botanical Garden and RHS)." RHS does not lead with "Virginia bluebells" — its page title is "Mertensia virginica | Virginian bluebells" (Virginian, with an n), which the note itself quotes correctly two clauses earlier and then contradicts. Only ONE of the three dedicated pages (MoBOT) leads with the exact string "Virginia bluebells". Sub-claim audit: (a) "NC State Extension's dedicated page lists its common-name set starting with 'Blue and Pink Ladies'" — CORRECT and cited; the live list runs Blue and Pink Ladies, Bluebells, Chiming Bells, Eastern Bluebells, Kentucky Bluebells, Lungwort Oysterleaf, Mertensia, Roanoke Bells, Smooth Lungwort, Virginia Bluebells, Virginia Cowslip, Virginia Spiderwort. (b) MoBOT "Common Name: Virginia bluebells" — CORRECT and cited. (c) RHS title "Mertensia virginica | Virginian bluebells" — CORRECT and cited, verified against the raw <title>. (d) "NC State's list ordering is alphabetical rather than a stated primary name" — TRUE but uncited; it is directly checkable from the twelve-name list above and can stand as an observation on the already-cited list. (e) "the name led by two of the three" — WRONG; drop it, do not re-cite it. Corrected wording for the final sentence: "'Virginia bluebells' is used here as the common_name because Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated page states it as a single primary name ('Common Name: Virginia bluebells') and leads its own common-name list with it, and RHS leads with the near-identical spelling variant 'Virginian bluebells'; NC State's twelve-name list is ordered alphabetically rather than by a stated primary name, which is why 'Blue and Pink Ladies' heads it." No material omission otherwise — the note does disclose both competing lead names.

water_regime — removed on audit: keep_moist is read off a soil adjective and is propped up by a structured field that does not corroborate it. Its only prose support is MoBOT's trailing preference clause "Prefers moist, rich soils." — quoted in isolation, with the sentence that immediately precedes it on the same page ("Easily grown in average, medium, well-drained soils in part shade to full shade.") dropped from the water_regime evidence, even though the record quotes that full sentence under soil_drainage. That is a dropped scope. Worse, the other citation is MoBOT's structured "Water: Medium" — the MIDDLE band of MoBOT's Dry / Dry to medium / Medium / Medium to wet / Wet scale — presented as if it supports the wettest available token. It does not; it is at best neutral and reads as tension, and nothing in unknowns discloses that tension. There is also an internal inconsistency: the record maps RHS's "moist but well-drained" to moderate drainage (correctly), then treats the same moisture language as justifying keep_moist without saying why the two readings diverge. The value may well survive repair — the WaterRegime enum has no middle token (keep_moist, keep_barely_moist, dry_surface_between, dry_thoroughly_between) and four sources use the word "moist" — but as cited it is not established. Repair: re-ground keep_moist on the species-specific moisture statements rather than the Medium band, using NC State's structured "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage / Moist" and RHS's structured "Moisture: Moist but well–drained" (both verified verbatim), relabel the "Water: Medium" citation so it is not presented as support, and add an unknowns entry disclosing that MoBOT's structured Water field places this mid-scale and that MoBOT's Culture lead is "average, medium, well-drained soils." Separately, consider whether keep_moist needs a dormancy qualifier: this plant is fully dormant from mid-summer, and a year-round keep-moist instruction is care guidance no source gives for the dormant half of the year — cool_rest_note flags the gap, but the water field itself carries no such scoping.

water_regime keep_moist rests on NC State's 'Moist' drainage tag, RHS's 'moist but well-drained' Moisture field and MOBOT's 'Prefers moist, rich soils'; MOBOT's structured Water field places the species mid-scale ('Water: Medium') and its Culture lead is 'average, medium, well-drained soils' -- disclosed as a counterpoint.

outdoor_sun_exposure — FLAGGED on audit (left as-is, needs manual review before landing): REFUTED on one entry only: drop "part_sun"; keep "part_shade" and "full_shade". Correct value: ["part_shade", "full_shade"].

Three separate defects converge on part_sun, and it rests on one citation (cit 10) alone:

(a) RELABELED QUOTE. The Clemson quote is verbatim -- I confirmed the page reads "Grow in light shade to full shade throughout South Carolina except for the coast." But the quote says "light shade," not part sun. The claim label "supports outdoor_sun_exposure part_sun (light shade) through full_shade" performs the mapping inside the parenthetical and presents it as if the source said it. Light shade is at or below partial shade on this catalog's ladder, not above it; mapping it to part_sun brightens the plant by a full step.

(b) CONDITIONAL CLAUSE. The sentence is geographically conditional -- "throughout South Carolina except for the coast" -- i.e. Clemson explicitly carves out a region where this guidance does not hold. A value resting on a conditional clause should go.

(c) CONTRADICTED BY BOTH STRUCTURED FIELDS. NC State's Light field for this exact species carries exactly three tags and no others: "Dappled Sunlight (Shade through upper canopy all day); Deep shade (Less than 2 hours to no direct sunlight); Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)" -- there is no Partial Sun or Full Sun tag. RHS's Position field is "Full shade, Partial shade" and nothing more. Two structured sources cap this species at partial shade; a single hedged prose sentence should not outvote both.

Also note the record never used the strongest available part_shade citation. NC State carries the literal tag "Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)" for this species, which supports part_shade directly; the record instead leans on the Dappled Sunlight tag. part_shade is not in doubt (RHS Position plus two NC State tags), but at repair time add that tag as a citation.

One further trap correctly avoided, worth confirming: UMD's lady fern page says "prefers full to partial shade; somewhat tolerant of sunlight as long as soil moisture remains high" -- that is a tolerance clause AND it is about the sibling species Athyrium asplenioides. It must not be used to rescue part_sun.

outdoor_sun_exposure: an earlier part_sun entry rested only on Clemson's 'light shade', which maps at or below partial shade; NC State's Light field and RHS's Position field both cap this species at partial shade.

records.name_note: RHS titles its profile 'North America wild oats' and lists 'northern sea oats, sea oats, spangle grass' as other common names, with 'river oats' absent from every RHS name field; RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden both record the synonym Uniola latifolia. unknowns: Admissible sources disagree on soil pH tolerance: NC State tags the species '#acidic soils intolerant,' while RHS's structured pH field lists Acid, Alkaline, and Neutral as all acceptable. Because the two sources conflict, soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null rather than picking a side.

Soil-moisture framing varies by source: RHS's structured Moisture field reads 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained' and NC State tags 'Moist' and 'Occasionally Wet,' both consistent with moderate drainage, but Clemson HGIC (The Fall Color of River Oats) frames the species as wanting consistently wet, very moist placement, saying it performs best in wet soil. soil_drainage is recorded as moderate on the weight of RHS and NC State, but the wetter Clemson framing is noted here rather than silently discarded.

No admissible source discusses toxicity to cats or dogs for this species at all -- there is no Poison/toxicity section on the NC State page and no Potentially harmful/Pets field on the RHS page -- so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than assumed non-toxic.

No admissible source gives numeric temperature ranges, humidity requirements, a chill-damage onset temperature, or foot-candle light levels for this species; only USDA hardiness zones are given (NC State: 5a-9b; Missouri Botanical Garden: zone 3-8), which per instructions is a hardiness rating, not a damage-onset temperature, so all of these fields are left null.

No admissible source frames watering for this in-ground perennial grass as a check-dryness or interval-based regime, so water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, and water_dormant_days_est are all left null.
No admissible source gives fertilizer guidance for this species, so all fertilize_* fields are left null.

Per the task's flag on aggressive self-seeding: NC State's species page states the plant 'can be a bit weedy as it self seeds easily' and warns gardeners to 'Watch its placement especially in smaller gardens as may spread aggressively by rhizomes and seeds.' Missouri Botanical Garden's Culture note likewise says it 'Self-seeds and may spread aggressively,' and its Uses note recommends naturalizing or mass plantings in home landscapes 'due to its tendency to spread.' Clemson HGIC frames the same rhizome spread positively, as erosion and sediment control along streambanks, rather than as a weediness warning. No schema field captures aggressive self-seeding or spread, so it is recorded here as decision-relevant for gardeners choosing this plant.

is_houseplant is recorded as false on the consistent outdoor/landscape framing across all three profile sources (USDA hardiness zones, naturalized/streamside garden uses, RHS's outdoor Position/Aspect/Exposure fields); no admissible source explicitly states the plant is unsuitable indoors, so this reflects the plant's outdoor-only profile rather than a direct statement to that effect.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good and direct_sun_hours_max are left null: no admissible source gives species-specific foot-candle figures, and NC State's 2-6 hour figure for its Partial Shade tag is the site-wide generic legend for that light category rather than species-specific prose, per instructions.

name_note — removed on audit: Refuted on one wrong sub-claim plus a material omission, though most of the bundle checks out. COVERED AND ACCURATE (verified verbatim, keep as-is): RHS titles the profile "Chasmanthium latifolium | North America wild oats" (exact <title>); RHS's "Other common names" paragraph reads exactly "northern sea oats, sea oats, spangle grass" and river oats is genuinely absent from every RHS name field; RHS Synonyms is "Uniola latifolia"; MOBOT's Noteworthy Characteristics contains "This grass was once known as Uniola latifolia"; NC State does publish parallel common-name alias pages, and https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/chasmanthium-latifolium/common-name/river-oats/ returns HTTP 200 with the exact title "River Oats - Chasmanthium latifolium" (siblings "Northern Sea Oats - Chasmanthium latifolium" and "Inland Sea Oats - Chasmanthium latifolium" also return 200, so that sub-claim is sound; there is at least a fourth, "Indian Wood Oats - Chasmanthium latifolium", so "one titled River Oats and others titled Northern Sea Oats and Inland Sea Oats" understates the set but says nothing false). WRONG — drop, do not re-cite: "Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder gives its single structured Common Name field as 'northern sea oats'" mis-describes the source's structure. MOBOT's page carries the "Common Name: northern sea oats" line AND an expandable "Common Names" list of eleven names rendered on the same page — verbatim: "northern sea oats, Indian woodoats, North America wild oats, sea oats, spangel grass, river oats, creek oats, Indian sea-oats, inland oats, wild oats, woodland oats" (MOBOT's own spelling, "spangel"). River oats is the sixth entry. In a note whose entire subject is which sources do and do not carry "river oats," calling MOBOT's structure "single" implies MOBOT does not recognize the name, which is false. UNCITED BUT TRUE — the material omission: name_note says NC State "does not designate a single primary name among them," which is fair for the alias-page layer, but it omits that NC State's base species page has its own structured "Common Name(s):" field listing six names alphabetically — Indian Wood Oats, Inland Sea Oats, Northern Sea Oats, River Oats, Wild Oats, Wood-oat — mirrored in the H1 parenthetical, and that the same page's prose leads with the queried name: "River Oats is a native, clump-forming, upright grass in the Poaceae (grass) family." With common_name landing as "Northern Sea Oats," a reader deserves to know that of the three sources one leads with that name, one leads with "North America wild oats," and the third runs its prose on "River Oats." CORRECTED WORDING: "Admissible sources split on the lead common name for this species. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder heads its profile with 'Common Name: northern sea oats,' though the same page's expandable Common Names list carries eleven names — 'northern sea oats, Indian woodoats, North America wild oats, sea oats, spangel grass, river oats, creek oats, Indian sea-oats, inland oats, wild oats, woodland oats' — river oats among them. RHS titles its dedicated species profile 'Chasmanthium latifolium | North America wild oats' and lists 'northern sea oats, sea oats, spangle grass' as other common names; river oats does not appear among RHS's names at all. NC State's Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox lists six names alphabetically in its 'Common Name(s):' field — Indian Wood Oats, Inland Sea Oats, Northern Sea Oats, River Oats, Wild Oats, Wood-oat — and publishes a parallel alias page for each, so its structured field designates no single primary name; its description prose, however, runs on River Oats: 'River Oats is a native, clump-forming, upright grass in the Poaceae (grass) family.' RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden both also record the older synonym Uniola latifolia."

normalizations: 2026-09-02: thirty-second batch (overnight throttle; 1.22M subagent tokens) -- a native woodland set: Foamflower, Canadian Wild Ginger, Solomon's Seal, Virginia Bluebells, Lady Fern, and Northern Sea Oats (researched as River Oats; landed under MOBOT's Common Name line, with the name_note recording that river oats sits sixth in MOBOT's own eleven-name list and that NC State publishes a River Oats alias page). land_check.py and covered.py ran clean; verify_quotes.py 78/79 reachable quotes, the miss a benign RHS title-plus-list. Repairs, each from the auditor's live-verified text: Canadian Wild Ginger's toxicity citation had truncated NC State's 'Poison Part: Leaves, Roots, Stems' to 'Leaves' -- the rhizome being the part people dig up as a ginger substitute -- and its RHS name citation carried a Position-field quote; both citations corrected, prose kept. Solomon's Seal's toxicity_detail restored with NC State's exact preparation times ('boiled for 10 minutes' / 'boiled for 20 minutes'), its full four-trait Plant Type list, its fruit-only poison-part scope disclosed against RHS's unrestricted 'Harmful if eaten', and its outdoor_sun_exposure narrowed to shade after both North American structured fields excluded full sun (only UK-calibrated RHS lists it); toxic_to_pets=true rests on RHS naming dogs.
